chapter.title: ooSQLite Specific Functions
chapter.para: Almost all of the fuctions in the Classic Rexx interface of ooSQLite have a one-to-one mapping with the SQLite API functions. A few functions are unique to ooSQLite. These functions are used to provide SQLite functionality that does not directly translate into Rexx. All functions of this type use a naming convention of ooSQLiteXxxxx(), while all functions that map directly to SQLite functions use a naming convention of oosqlXxxx(). The ooSQLite unique functions are documented in this chapter.

section.title: &added11;ooSQLiteEncryptionAvailable
section.para: Tells whether the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses can encrypt databases.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
Returns true if SQLite was built with an encryption extension, and false otherwise. The SQLite embedded in ooSQLite is built without one, so the routine returns false.
The routine tests the SQLITE_HAS_CODEC compile-time option, which the encryption extensions for SQLite used to define. Plain SQLite has no encryption.
This routine is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API.
The encryptionAvailable method of the ooSQLite class does the same.
This routine was in ooSQLite before version 1.1, but it was not documented.

This example tests whether encryption is available:
say 'Encryption available:' ooSQLiteEncryptionAvailable() /* Output: Encryption available: 0 */

section.title: &changed11;ooSQLiteEnquote
section.para: Converts the supplied Rexx value(s) into SQL literals. This function is useful to help construct SQL statements. The specified Rexx object(s) are converted to SQL literals by adding single quotes to the beginning and end of the string value of the object, escaping single quotes within the string value of the object, and changing the .nil object to SQL NULL.

listitem.para:
The single argument is:
values [optional]
A Rexx object, or an array-like stem of Rexx objects, to be converted to SQL literals. If this argument is omitted then NULL is returned.
The string value of the specified object(s) as a SQL literal, or a comma separated list of SQL literals.

The ooSQLiteEnquote routine accepts a single argument values. If values is a stem, then it must be a stem containing tails that are positive whole number indexes. The stem can contain tails 1 through N where N is the count of values to convert, and must contain the tail 0 whose value is N. Any tail 1 through N that is not assigned a value is converted to SQL NULL. Any tail 1 through N whose assigned value is the .nil object is also converted to SQL NULL. For all other tails 1 through N, the value assigned to the tail is converted to a string enclosed in single quotes. If the string contains single quotes, those single quotes are escaped. If the stem contains any other tails, other than 0 through N, those tails are ignored. If N is greater than 1, then each converted value is added to the string with a comma used as a separator.

If values is not a stem, then it is taken to be a single value to be converted, and is converted in the same manner as a single tail of a stem is converted, as described above. This implies that if values is omitted altogether, it is converted to SQL NULL.

&changed11;The result has no length limit, whatever the number of values. Before ooSQLite 1.1, a stem with more than one value gave a result of at most 4095 characters, cut without an error when the last value went over, and a stem with a single value gave an unpredictable result. When N is 0, NULL is returned.
The functionality of the ooSQLiteEnQuote function is similar to that of the sqlite3_mprintf SQLite API

This example shows how the enquote function can be ussed to create SQL INSERT statements that are not prone to SQL Injection flaws:
r1.0 = 4 r1.1 = "Tom" r1.2 = "Hanks" r1.4 = "male"
r2.0 = 4 r2.1 = "Mike" r2.3 = "555-9988" r2.4 = .nil
sql1 = "INSERT INTO my_table (fName, lName, phone, gender) VALUES("ooSQLiteEnquote(r1.)");" sql2 = "INSERT INTO my_table (fName, lName, phone, gender) VALUES("ooSQLiteEnquote(r2.)");"
say sql1 say sql2
/* Output would be:
INSERT INTO my_table (fName, lName, phone, gender) VALUES('Tom', 'Hanks', NULL, 'male'); INSERT INTO my_table (fName, lName, phone, gender) VALUES('Mike', NULL, '555-9988', NULL);
*/
This example shows a conversion for a single string that has an apostrophe within it:
str = "It's a happy day!" say ooSQLiteEnquote(str)
/* Output would be:
'It''s a happy day!'
*/

section.title: ooSQLiteMerge
section.para: Combines several flags into one value, with a bitwise or.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
arg [optional]
Any number of whole numbers, normally constants of the ooSQLiteConstants class, such as the OPEN_ flags. None of them can be omitted between the first one and the last one.
The bitwise or of all the arguments: a number with every bit that is set in any of them. With no arguments, 0 is returned; with one, that argument.
Rexx has no operator for a bitwise or of numbers. The flags of SQLite are powers of 2, so adding distinct flags gives the same result, but adding a flag twice does not; ooSQLiteMerge is always right.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if an argument is not a whole number, and 88.901 if one is omitted, as in ooSQLiteMerge(a, , b).
This routine is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API.
The merge method of the ooSQLiteConstants class does the same.

This example opens the database of the connection db a second time, read only and without the mutex of the connection, and tries to change it:
file = oosqlDbFileName(db, 'main') flags = ooSQLiteMerge(.ooSQLite~OPEN_READONLY, .ooSQLite~OPEN_NOMUTEX) say 'Flags:' flags rc = oosqlOpen(file, 'readOnly', flags) say 'Delete:' oosqlExec(readOnly, "DELETE FROM foods;") call oosqlClose readOnly /* Output: Flags: 32769 Delete: SQLite Error: rc = 8, attempt to write a readonly database */

section.title: ooSQLiteRegisterBuiltin
section.para: Registers one of the extensions built into ooSQLite with a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
name [required]
The name of the extension: base64, csv, ieee754, nextChar, percentile, regExp, rot13, spellFix, toType, or wholeNumber. Case is not significant.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error.

The extensions come from the SQLite source tree, and are linked into the ooSQLite library: they do not need to be loaded with oosqlLoadExtension. An extension registered with this routine is available only on the given connection, until it is closed.
Raises a syntax error if name is not the name of a builtin extension.

The error message of the extension, if it gives one, is not recorded in the connection, so oosqlErrMsg does not return it. It is stored in the .local directory, with the index ROUTINEERRORMESSAGE, and can be retrieved as .routineErrorMessage. Each call to ooSQLiteRegisterBuiltin sets it to the empty string first. oosqlLoadExtension uses the same entry. Being in .local, it is shared by all the threads of the interpreter instance.
The registerBuiltin method of the ooSQLExtensions class does the same, and can register several extensions at once.

This example registers the base64 extension, and uses its SQL function to decode a string:
rc = ooSQLiteRegisterBuiltin(db, 'base64') if rc <> .ooSQLite~OK then do say 'Error' rc':' .routineErrorMessage return rc end rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT base64('SGVsbG8gd29ybGQh') AS text;", .true) say rows.1['TEXT'] /* Output: Hello world! */

section.title: ooSQLiteVersion
section.para: Returns the version of ooSQLite, or of the SQLite library it uses, in one of several formats.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
type [optional]
The format, one of these keywords. Only the first letter is checked, and case is not significant:
OneLine: the version of ooSQLite on one line, such as ooSQLite Version 1.0.2.13107 (64 bit). This is the default.
Compact: the version number of ooSQLite, such as 1.0.2.13107.
Full: several lines, with the versions of ooSQLite, ooRexx, and SQLite, the date ooSQLite was built, and its copyright.
LibVersion: the version of SQLite, as oosqlLibVersion returns it.
Number: the version of SQLite as a number, as oosqlLibVersionNumber returns it.
SourceID: the source identifier of SQLite, as oosqlSourceID returns it.
The version, in the format asked for.
This is the routine that returns the version of ooSQLite; oosqlVersion, despite its name, returns the version of SQLite. The Full format is useful in problem reports.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if type does not start with one of the letters O, C, F, L, N, or S.
This routine is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API.
The version method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example displays the version in several formats. The output depends on the build:
say ooSQLiteVersion() say ooSQLiteVersion('Compact') say ooSQLiteVersion('LibVersion') say ooSQLiteVersion('F') /* Output might be: ooSQLite Version 1.0.2.13107 (64 bit) 1.0.2.13107 3.52.0 ooSQLite: ooSQLite Version 1.0.2.13107 (64 bit) Built Oct 18 2026 13:47:21 Copyright (c) 2012-2026 Rexx Language Association. All rights reserved.
Rexx: Open Object Rexx Version 5.3.0
SQLite: SQLite Library Version 3.52.0 2026-03-06 16:01:44 */
